newsitem.title: FRANCE: Germany may fail Maastricht - ex-Buba head Poehl.
newsitem.headline: Germany may fail Maastricht - ex-Buba head Poehl.

text.p: Germany looks unlikely to meet Maastricht treaty criteria on debt and deficits, posing a tough problem for the government on the road to European monetary union, former Bundesbank head Karl Otto Poehl said on Tuesday.

He told a conference that while his starting assumption was that the euro would be launched on schedule in January 1999, "it could still be possible that the whole exercise will be postponed or may even fail."
"What appears particularly worrying is the fact that Germany is far away from meeting the (Maastricht) target," Poehl said.

The most prominent think-tanks had predicted that Germany would overshoot Maastricht treaty requirements limiting public deficits to three percent of gross domestic product and debt to 60 percent of GDP.
All of these had based their forecast on what Poehl said he considered optimistic assumptions.
"Without a considerable acceleration of economic growth, Germany will fail to meet the deficit criteria," he said. "It could happen that we meet these targets, but I don't think it's very likely."
Germany however was in the difficult situation of having told its European partners and its own people the Maastricht treaty must be interpreted strictly. "It's a little ugly."

"It's a political and psychological problem in Germany," he said, adding that the German public would lose all confidence in the monetary union project if the government accepted a political solution by fudging the criteria.
"I have no idea how the government will solve this very delicate problem," he said.

He added that he believed if there were a referendum in Germany today on monetary union, Germans would vote against it. "So far amazingly we have not had much political opposition despite the fact that there is a majority against it."
But he said the risks of failure or delay in launching the euro were greater than the dangers of going ahead.
"A postponement or failure would at this stage imply a severe setback in the process of European integration which would be hard to repair," he said.
Germany would look more to eastern Europe, while France, for a while, would give up its "franc fort" policy of keeping the franc stable against the mark.
"On balance the chances are bigger than the risks and we should try to go ahead with this experiment," Poehl, who was speaking in English, said.
